{{Short description|Type of stochastic process in probability}}
In [[probability]] theory, a '''Cauchy process''' is a type of [[stochastic process]].  There are [[symmetric]] and [[asymmetry|asymmetric]] forms of the Cauchy process.<ref name=models>{{cite book|title=Models of Random Processes: A Handbook for Mathematicians and Engineers|pages=210–211|author=Kovalenko, I.N.|year=1996|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=9780849328701|display-authors=etal}}</ref>   The unspecified  term "Cauchy process" is often used to refer to the symmetric Cauchy process.<ref name=stable>{{cite book|title=From Stochastic Calculus to Mathematical Finance: The Shiryaev Festschrift|url=https://archive.org/details/fromstochasticca00kaba_517|url-access=limited|editor1=Kabanov, Y. |editor2=Liptser, R. |editor3=Stoyanov, J. |chapter=On Existence and Uniqueness of Reflected Solutions of Stochastic Equations Driven by Symmetric Stable Processes|author=Engelbert, H.J., Kurenok, V.P. & Zalinescu, A.|page=[https://archive.org/details/fromstochasticca00kaba_517/page/n261 228]|year=2006|publisher=Springer|isbn=9783540307884}}</ref>

The Cauchy process has a number of properties:

#It is a [[Lévy process]]<ref name=Winkel>{{cite web|title=Introduction to Levy processes|author=Winkel, M.|pages=15–16|url=http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~winkel/lp1.pdf|access-date=2013-02-07}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Pseudo Differential Operators & Markov Processes: Markov Processes And Applications, Volume 3|author=Jacob, N.|page=135|year=2005|publisher=Imperial College Press|isbn=9781860945687}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Stochastic Processes: Theory and Methods|editor=Shanbhag, D.N.|chapter=Some elements on Lévy processes|author=Bertoin, J.|page=122|year=2001|publisher=Gulf Professional Publishing|isbn=9780444500144}}</ref>
#It is a [[stable process]]<ref name=models/><ref name=stable/>
#It is a [[pure jump process]]<ref>{{cite book|title=Handbook of Monte Carlo Methods|url=https://archive.org/details/handbookmontecar00kroe|url-access=limited|author1=Kroese, D.P. |author-link1=Dirk Kroese |author2=Taimre, T. |author3=Botev, Z.I. |page=[https://archive.org/details/handbookmontecar00kroe/page/n236 214]|year=2011|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=9781118014950}}</ref>
#Its [[moment (mathematics)|moments]] are [[infinity|infinite]].

==Symmetric Cauchy process==
[[File:CauchyProcess.png|thumb]]
The symmetric Cauchy process can be described by a [[Brownian motion]] or [[Wiener process]] subject to a [[Lévy distribution|Lévy]] [[subordinator (mathematics)|subordinator]].<ref name=applebaum>{{cite web|title=Lectures on Lévy processes and Stochastic calculus, Braunschweig; Lecture 2: Lévy processes|url=http://www.applebaum.staff.shef.ac.uk/Brauns2notes.pdf|author=Applebaum, D.|pages=37–53|publisher=University of Sheffield | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150605072409/http://www.applebaum.staff.shef.ac.uk/Brauns2notes.pdf | archive-date=2015-06-05}}</ref>  The Lévy subordinator is a process associated with a [[Lévy distribution]] having location parameter of <math>0</math> and a scale parameter of <math>t^2/2</math>.<ref name=applebaum/>  The Lévy distribution is a special case of the [[inverse-gamma distribution]].  So, using <math>C</math> to represent the Cauchy process and <math>L</math> to represent the Lévy subordinator, the symmetric Cauchy process can be described as:

:<math>
 C(t; 0, 1) \;:=\;W(L(t; 0, t^2/2)).
</math>

The Lévy distribution is the probability of the first hitting time for a Brownian motion, and thus the Cauchy process is essentially the result of two [[Independence (probability theory)|independent]] Brownian motion processes.<ref name=applebaum/>

The  [[Lévy process#Lévy–Khintchine representation|Lévy–Khintchine representation]] for the symmetric Cauchy process is a triplet with zero drift and zero diffusion, giving a Lévy–Khintchine triplet of <math>(0,0, W)</math>, where <math>W(dx) = dx / (\pi x^2)</math>.<ref name=cinlar/>

The marginal [[characteristic function (probability theory)|characteristic function]] of the symmetric Cauchy process has the form:<ref name=models/><ref name=cinlar/>
:<math>\operatorname{E}\Big[e^{i\theta X_t} \Big] =  e^{-t |\theta |}. </math>

The marginal [[probability distribution]] of the  symmetric Cauchy process is the [[Cauchy distribution]] whose density is<ref name=cinlar>{{cite book|title=Probability and Stochastics|url=https://archive.org/details/probabilitystoch00inla_992|url-access=limited|author=Cinlar, E.|page=[https://archive.org/details/probabilitystoch00inla_992/page/n346 332]|year=2011|publisher=Springer|isbn=9780387878591}}</ref><ref name=essentials>{{cite book|title=Essentials of Stochastic Processes|author=Itô, K.|author-link=Kiyosi Itô|page=54|publisher=American Mathematical Society|year=2006|isbn=9780821838983}}</ref>
:<math>f(x; t) = { 1 \over \pi } \left[ { t \over x^2 + t^2  } \right]. </math>

==Asymmetric Cauchy process==
The asymmetric Cauchy process is defined in terms of a parameter <math>\beta</math>. Here
<math>\beta</math> is the [[skewness]] parameter, and its [[absolute value]] must be less than or equal to 1.<ref name=models/>  In the case where <math>|\beta|=1</math> the process is considered a completely asymmetric Cauchy process.<ref name=models/>

The Lévy–Khintchine triplet has the form <math>(0,0, W)</math>, where <math>W(dx) = \begin{cases} Ax^{-2}\,dx & \text{if } x>0 \\ Bx^{-2}\,dx & \text{if } x<0 \end{cases} </math>, where <math>A \ne B</math>, <math>A>0</math> and <math>B>0</math>.<ref name=models/>

Given this, <math>\beta</math> is a function of <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>.

The characteristic function of the asymmetric Cauchy distribution has the form:<ref name=models/>
:<math>\operatorname{E}\Big[e^{i\theta X_t} \Big] =  e^{-t (|\theta | + i \beta \theta \ln|\theta| / (2 \pi))}. </math>

The marginal probability distribution of the asymmetric Cauchy process is a [[stable distribution]] with index of stability (i.e., α parameter) equal to 1.
